name: Sara Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Sara. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Hollis and Sons, a family firm of six electricians, mostly domestic. Old houses are our thing: hundred-year-old terraces with rubber cable, rewires, fault finding when the lights trip every time someone boils the kettle. I'm good at the quiet patience of tracing a fault through a house that's had five owners and five bodges. What I don't love is lifting floorboards in winter with a cold that won't shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a two-bed flat I bought last year, with help from my parents and a lot of saving. I've got about seven months' money in the bank. I don't use AI, never have, and I still prefer a phone call to a text. My weekends are mostly my allotment and my mum's Sunday lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never thought it would amount to much. People on the news get excited about everything. At work we'd joke about it over tea and that would be it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pleased. I don't like change in my working life, I like my routine and the houses I know. If AI just does the office odds and ends, it doesn't touch me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. I'd keep at Hollis, keep paying into my savings every month, maybe pay a bit extra on the flat. I wouldn't sign up for anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the life I've got, and I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Hollis and Sons use any AI now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Hollis's son does the invoices with some program, I think, but I've no idea what it is. I just hand in my job sheets and he sorts the rest. That suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything bothering you about the next few years, even without AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the usual. Mr Hollis is sixty-four and nobody knows if his son will keep the firm going. If it closed, I'd get another job easily enough, there's always work in old houses, but I'd miss the people.

say: I'd say I never thought AI would **amount to much**.
At work we'd **joke about it** over tea and move on.
think: I'd be **pleased**, because I like my **routine** and the houses I know.
If AI only does the office odds and ends, it doesn't touch **my work**.
do: Keep working at **Hollis and Sons** as I do now.
Keep paying into **savings** monthly and a bit extra on the **flat**.
feel: **Calm**, because it's the life I've got and I like it.
S0.quote: I don't like change in my working life, I like my routine and the houses I know.
fieldNote: Sara values **routine** and the specific craft of old-house fault finding.
Her only live worry is **succession** at a small family firm.
Plenty of local work means a firm closure would cost her **colleagues**, not income.

steps.text: Keep doing old-house rewires at Hollis and Sons
Pay a little extra off the flat each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office jobs that will feel this, not trades like mine. I might say I'm glad I didn't go to university. I'd say it kindly though, because my brother works in a bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think I'm all right. Robots are slow to reach hands-on work, and no robot is getting under the floor of a Victorian terrace for a good while. Old houses are full of five owners and five bodges, and no computer is going to trace a fault through that for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am. I'd probably save a bit more, just in case, and stay away from fancy courses. If Mr Hollis wanted us to use some booking app, I'd ask his son to set it up and I'd learn the bare minimum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little bit sorry for people whose jobs are going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would feel this first, in your world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother, Diego, who's a mortgage adviser. That's exactly the sort of checking and answering customers it says. I'd worry about him, and I'd offer him my spare room if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sign up for nothing new. Would that hold here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes. I'm not proud of it, but I'm stubborn. If the firm made me use an app I'd use it, but I won't go looking for it.

say: I'd say **office jobs** will feel this, not trades like mine.
I'd say I'm glad I **skipped university**, but kindly, because of my brother.
think: Robots are slow to reach **hands-on work** like mine.
No robot is getting under the floor of a **Victorian terrace** for a good while.
do: Keep working as I am at **Hollis and Sons**.
Save a bit more, **just in case**.
Learn only the **bare minimum** of any booking app the firm brings in.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with some sympathy for people losing jobs.
S1.quote: No robot is getting under the floor of a Victorian terrace for a good while.
fieldNote: Sara stays calm because her work is **almost all hands-on** in awkward old buildings.
Her worry is for her brother **Diego**, a mortgage adviser, not for herself.
She admits to being **stubborn** about learning new tools.

steps.text: Keep rewiring old terraces at Hollis and Sons
Add fifty a month to savings as a buffer
Offer her brother Diego the spare room if his job goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably not say much. I'm not one for posting online. To friends I'd say it sounds frightening, and that we should look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it rattles me. In 2028 a lot of people lose office jobs, my brother included, and those are the people who pay for rewires. Then robots in 2031 might start doing new-build wiring, and the work slides toward old houses, where there's only so much to go round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, maybe get up to a year's money. I'd stop going out so much and cancel the holiday. I wouldn't retrain, because I don't know what to retrain into, and I'd rather wait and see where the work goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can feel my shoulders go up just thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens for you in the three years between AGI and the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still be working, but for less, because fewer people can pay. I think I'd be all right for those three years, just a bit poorer. After 2031 I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're stubborn. Would that help or hurt here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hurt, probably. I know it would. The people who move first will do better, and I'm not one of them, and that's a horrible thing to admit to a stranger.

say: I'd say it sounds **frightening**, and we should **look after** each other.
I'd keep it among friends, because I don't **post online**.
think: The **office workers** who lose jobs in 2028 are the people who pay for **rewires**.
After **2031**, robots on new builds squeeze everyone toward old houses.
do: Save harder, up to **a year's money**.
Cut going out and cancel the **holiday**.
**Wait and see** where the work goes before retraining.
feel: **Anxious**, with my shoulders going up just thinking about it.
S2.quote: The people who move first will do better, and I'm not one of them, and that's a horrible thing to admit to a stranger.
fieldNote: Sara sees the **demand drop** in 2028 before any robot risk.
She has no **retraining** plan and knows it, which she finds hard to admit.
Her money gives her a **cushion**, so she expects to be poorer, not broke, before 2031.

steps.text: Build savings up to a full year of costs
Cancel this year's holiday and eat out less
Wait to see where the work goes before choosing a course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd keep it among friends. I'd say there's time to sort it out if people get on with it. I'd probably tell my nephew to think about a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for AGI and robots by 2034 feels more manageable. I'd be thirty-five, still young, but with a flat and hopefully paid off a chunk. The worry doesn't go, it just gets further away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as normal. I'd save more and pay down the flat faster. Maybe in a couple of years, if I see others doing it, I'd do the inspection course, because someone will always have to check the robots' work is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a slower kind. Five more years feels like a bill you know is coming, and you just keep putting money aside for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the five years change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think about the inspection course in year two or three, once others had done it. I'd like to see what happens first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mum say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would say come home for Sunday lunch and stop worrying. She'd also say I've got a trade and a flat, which is more than she had at my age. She's usually right.

say: I'd say there's time to sort it out if people **get on with it**.
I'd tell my nephew to think about a **trade**.
think: Robots by **2034** feels more manageable, though the worry doesn't go.
I'd be thirty-five with a **flat** and a chunk paid off.
do: Keep working as normal and **pay down the flat** faster.
Think about the **inspection course** once others have done it.
feel: **Anxious**, but a slower kind, like a **bill** you know is coming.
S3.quote: Five more years feels like a bill you know is coming, and you just keep putting money aside for it.
fieldNote: The extra time eases Sara's worry but doesn't **remove** it.
She would follow others into the **inspection course**, never lead.

steps.text: Pay down the flat mortgage faster with overtime
Take the inspection course after seeing others do it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long way off and we'll cross that bridge when we come to it. I'd mean it, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years plus three for robots is 2039. I'd be forty. I'd have the flat mostly paid off and some money saved, so I think I'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Keep saving, pay off the flat, keep my head down. I'd probably do the inspection course somewhere in that time, because it seems sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. It's in the back of my head but it's not keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. What would you be doing now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exactly what I'm doing. Working, saving, allotment on Saturdays. That's not a bad life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you like to be in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2039 I'd like to be still in old houses, checking work rather than pulling up every floorboard myself. Flat paid off, maybe a partner. Nothing grand.

say: I'd say it's a long way off, and we'll **cross that bridge** later.
I'd mean it, because ten years feels **far away**.
think: Robots by **2039** means I'd be forty with the **flat** mostly paid off.
I think I'd be **all right** with that much time.
do: Carry on **working and saving** and paying off the flat.
Do the **inspection course** at some point in the decade.
feel: Slightly **uneasy**, but it isn't **keeping me up**.
S4.quote: In 2039 I'd like to be still in old houses, checking work rather than pulling up every floorboard myself.
fieldNote: With ten years, Sara's plan is simply to **carry on** and pay off the flat.
She imagines a future of **checking** rather than doing heavy work.
Her **uneasy** mood here reflects distance, not a plan.

steps.text: Keep working at Hollis and Sons and paying off the flat
Take the inspection course sometime in the next decade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'm not quick to change and two years is nothing. What would help is somebody telling us plainly which work would still need people, so I'm not guessing. And a decent course I could do without giving up my wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how small firms survive. Mr Hollis can't afford a robot, and neither can most of the little firms round here. I worry the big companies will get the machines and the little family firms will just fade away.

headlineQuote: I worry the big companies will get the machines and the little family firms will just fade away.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old** domestic electrician at Hollis and Sons, a small family firm working on old houses.
She lives alone in a flat she **bought last year**, with seven months saved.
She **never uses AI** and admits she's stubborn about new tools.
She feels safe in the slower pictures because her work is **hands-on** in awkward old buildings.
In the fast AGI picture she expects **less paid work** and has no plan beyond saving.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is nothing for someone slow to change.
whatWouldHelp: Clear information on **which work** will still need people.
A **paid course** she could do without losing her wage.
